https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/wild.title: Mya-Rose Craig: the cool new face of birdwatching
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/wild.text:
Mya-Rose Craig has been a committed “twitcher” and “birder” since she was a young girl (“twitching” involves the pursuit of a specific ornithological species, “birding” is casual spotting). Most weekends she is out in the countryside enjoying the wildlife. But last week the 18-year-old environmental activist, who is British-Bangladeshi, was spotted herself.
Her memoir, titled Birdgirl and the subject of a 14-way auction among British publishers, is rumoured to have sold for more than £250,000.
“Writing about birds and the environment is something I’ve done for years, so I was amazed that there was so much interest,” she says. “But with everything that’s going on in the world right now, perhaps people really are rediscovering the beauty and necessity of the natural world.”
The deal and her environmental activism are likely to cement Craig’s growing reputation as the “British Greta Thunberg”. Last month she went to the Arctic, just north of Svalbard, Norway, to take part in the most northerly “youth climate strike” protest to date. Craig travelled there on a Greenpeace ship, then balanced on an ice floe, placard in hand. While the lockdown paused the widespread youth climate strikes by British and other schools, she wanted to highlight the fact that, pandemic or not, the Arctic ice is reportedly melting faster than ever. In February she shared a platform with the Swedish activist in Bristol. “Greta is younger than me, but she has incredible power and presence,” Craig says. “I was just in awe.” She is wary of being compared to Thunberg. Spend an afternoon at the Craigs’ cottage and you find a reluctant figurehead. For her and her family, it really is all about the birds.
When the weather forecast brings news of an impending storm, the Craig family get excited. A storm off the Atlantic means high winds. High winds mean birds’ flight paths are interrupted. And living in the Somerset village of Compton Martin means that Craig is among the first to see the amazing avian life as it arrives.
“Of course I don’t want birds to get lost, but we live by Chew Valley Lake near Bristol, which is a really important nesting ground,” she says. “A lot of migrating birds come this way. I’ve been out birding in some really horrible weather, but the excitement of seeing a species you’ve never seen before never leaves you.”
Craig’s first bird — a lesser kestrel — was recorded before she was one. Her parents, Chris and Helena, and sister Ayesha, 30, have long been keen birders. After expeditions to 38 countries over seven continents Craig has spotted more than 5,000 of the world’s 10,738 species. In fact, her mother credits the hobby with saving the family.
In 2009 Helena was a partner in a law firm in Bristol. Her husband was often away working on international construction projects. Both worked long hours, and Ayesha often babysat her younger sister.
“When Mya was eight, she turned to me while we were walking in the Andes and said, ‘It’s been really nice getting to know you and dad. For a long time I thought Ayesha was my mother and you were just someone who came in to kiss me goodnight,’ ” Helena recalls. “That was a real wake-up call. Chris and I decided we’d take early retirement and spend more time with the children doing things we liked.”
In 2013 they went to Australia. In 2015 it was Uganda, Rwanda and Kenya. Last year they travelled to Brazil in search of the rare harpy eagle. “They are true wonders of nature. But there is a serious side,” Craig says. “Birding is so closely associated with issues around the environment. When we fly we pay for carbon offset, use local guides and stay in eco-tourism places run by indigenous people.”
“Birding” is a serious business in the UK too, especially when there is a “twitch” on. In 2009 Craig declared a “big year”, a birdwatcher term for attempting a personal record for bird spotting (or taking part in an informal competition) within a 12-month period. Her father kept a close eye on his pager: a device specifically intended to signal rare bird alerts. One evening in October news popped up about an odd-looking bird that had been spotted 300 miles away at Trow Quarry in South Shields, Tyne and Wear. After frantic discussion, a local expert identified the brown and yellow bird as an eastern crowned warbler, which normally breeds in Japan, Korea and China, and migrates to Malaysia and Indonesia.
In twitching terms this was like spotting Lord Lucan in the high street stroking his moustache. Only three previous sightings had been made of the bird in the whole of Europe since 1843, and it had never been seen in Britain. As a result a “mega-alert” went out. Craig, who was seven at the time, was asleep in bed. “It was crazy,” she recalls. “My dad woke me and my mum up just after midnight and we drove through the rest of the night to get a glimpse.”
They arrived at the quarry at dawn. There were already 300 other twitchers surrounding the bird, which had probably become disorientated on its migration.
“There’s a great feeling of comradeship with other birders on an occasion like that,” Craig says. “The older birdwatchers are good at protecting the bird. I’ve even heard of them mooting 24-hour patrols when a really rare species is spotted.”
With a bit of research on a global bird database called Avibase, the Craigs determine which countries play host to the species they have yet to see. It was this research that led to their first trip to South America in 2009. Craig’s school allowed her time off and she missed her friends. But there were greater obstacles: such as confronting her fear of heights and spiders.
In Ecuador she spent three days at the top of a 200ft-high bird-viewing platform that swayed in the wind. In Colombia she was forced to confront a species of jumping spider that was able to leap as high as her waist. Then there was a tarantula in Chile.
“That was the worst thing ever,” she says. “I’m someone who cares about wildlife, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t certain things that make me want to scream.”
However, perhaps most difficult of all has been dealing with racism in pursuit of the hobby she loves. In 2009 she was featured on a BBC documentary about birdwatching and in 2014 she began writing her Birdgirl blog, which has attracted almost five million visitors. Initially she was trolled, with some questioning the right of a young Muslim to enjoy birdwatching.
“I’ve grown up to be tough about it,” she says. “Some people think you’re arrogant or misguided for speaking up about birds, the environment or biodiversity. Is it a race thing? Is it because I’m a girl? I don’t know. I’ve seen how Greta [Thunberg] gets criticised, but she is amazingly strong. Like her, I really do focus on the fact that this is my generation’s future at stake.”
In 2015, with the help of her parents, she turned this cynicism on its head: she set about trying to attract more people from black and ethnic minorities into birdwatching and nature. She organised her first birdwatching camp on the Somerset Levels and a year later a Race Equality in Nature conference attended by the broadcaster Bill Oddie. This has evolved into the youth organisation Black2Nature, which attracts black and ethnic minority children to her weekend birdwatching and rambling camps. To date, more than 200 children aged between 8 and 19 have attended.
“I try to mix up the groups so that we have some inner-city children and some local enthusiasts. A lot of the children from inner cities have never even seen a sheep before, and it’s so lovely to see them get excited by nature. I started so young, I only became aware of how ‘white’ nature can seem when I was older, and it seems really sad that everyone doesn’t enjoy something that is so good for our mental health.”
Craig’s passion for birds has become the cornerstone of a complete world view. She has become a vegetarian for environmental reasons. And after a trip to Borneo during which the family drove for five hours through jungle cleared for palm oil plantations (there were no birds), she has become a fervent campaigner against palm oil overproduction. “Seeing what is happening to our world with your own eyes is really frightening.”
However, there are hopeful signs. A reduction in air and road traffic as a result of the Covid-19 “lockdown” has helped to reduce environmental pollution and regenerate biodiversity. “I know how terrible Covid has been for some people, but yes, lockdown has given parts of our biodiversity a breather. The great challenge is to make that recovery permanent.”
Craig qualified to “ring” birds when she was eight (you catch a bird in a “mist net” and, handling it carefully, place an aluminium ID ring on its foot for future observation) and recently she has begun to identify fully grown swallows, dunnocks and reed warblers that she first encountered as chicks. “These are birds that I ‘ringed’ years ago and that have migrated to Africa and back several times, so it’s great to see them thriving,” she says.
It has been a tumultuous 2020 so far. She was awarded an honorary doctorate in science by Bristol University, and yet, like many others, had to settle for predicted A-level results (she heads to Warwick University next year to read politics and international relations). Lockdown also ended her hopes of birding in the Isles of Scilly because of continued uncertainty over local travel restrictions.
Looking out into the woodland around her home, she warns of another big threat: cats. Global weather changes, habitat destruction, even bad wind turbine design, have taken their toll on bird populations, but cats remain enemy No 1. According to the RSPB cats kill about 27 million birds a year in the UK. “Oh, I love cats, but they are terrible for birds,” Craig says. “It’s my ambition to see the other half of the world’s bird species. Cats without bells on their collars only make that harder.”
WrenThese are one of the most underrated birds in the UK. They’re often considered boring, but I have always held a special place in my heart for wrens. Small and shy, creeping around hedges, they’re lovely when you get close up.
RedwingThis small thrush has a bold white stripe that wraps around the eye. It’s one of my favourite birds at this time of year because its rusty plumage brightens up bleak winter skies.
PintailI grew up with a lake as my local patch and pintails are a favourite of mine, with their chocolate-coloured heads and sharp, thin tails, after which they are named.
YellowhammerA stunning winter bird often found in farm hedges, the yellowhammer is one of Britain’s brighter birds and is always a highlight of winter for me.
WaxwingWaxwings always make me think of those perfectly crisp winter days. We once managed to track down a tree full of them. The joy of seeing this bird will never wear off.
RobinI love robins for the same reason most people do: they’re cute to look at and they’re friendly. This species is reliably in your garden year-round, perching in full view, showing off its lovely red breast.
KingfisherI love going out and spotting the brief flashes of iridescent colour as this beautiful bird darts around the water’s edge. It’s a British classic, loved by many.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Art review: Polly Morgan’s How to Behave at Home at the Bomb Factory; The Royal Academy’s Winter Exhibition
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
Polly Morgan has a new show. It’s her first solo display since 2012. And — brace yourselves — it’s got taxidermy in it. Dead snakes. Dead hedgehogs.
Further down the page I will be showering praise on Morgan’s exquisite manipulation of expired beasties, but as I’m not the kind of art critic who avoids the rapids when I’m kayaking, let’s start with the difficult stuff. Taxidermy is problematic. I know it. You know it.
In the Victorian world, where so many of Britain’s cultural norms made their debut, extinguishing wildlife was the done thing. You went to the colonies. You shot the bejesus out of anything that flew, ran, swung or slithered. And you stuffed it. Then you put it on your mantelpiece, where its task was to connect you with the paradisiacal past you lost when you stopped hunting and gathering and started shovelling coal into the furnaces of Bolton. We paved paradise. We put up a parking lot. The excitements of taxidermy lead all the way back to the Garden of Eden.
These days, of course, we need to stay mum about that. Declare yourself to be a taxidermy enthusiast and David Attenborough will be round to bash down the door while Extinction Rebellion set fire to the house. Today taxidermy is a cultural no-no. Except in the world of art.
Long before Damien Hirst stuffed his first shark, the symbolic manipulation of animal parts played a recurring role in the contortions of modernism. In the 1930s the surrealist Meret Oppenheim turned a teacup into something creepy by wrapping it in the fur of a gazelle. In the 1960s Joseph Beuys locked himself in a room with a stuffed hare and involved it in a noisy lament on Germany’s lost past. In the 1980s Denis Masi used screaming monkeys as pitch-perfect stand-ins for us.
In all these instances, the task handed to the preserved beasts was to remind us of our origins; to speak to the animal within. And in her small but perfectly formed display How to Behave at Home at a tiny gallery called the Bomb Factory (it’s just off the Holloway Road in north London, open Thursday to Sunday), Morgan continues these unsettling explorations.
What hits you first is the immaculate presentation; the immediate evidence of an OCD mind. Precise sculptures on plinths. Precise pictures on walls. The work may consist chiefly of dead animals, but its moods are pure, angelic, strikingly white.
Of the nine sculptures in the show, eight are not much bigger than a clock on a Victorian mantelpiece. Only one, the most brooding, is significantly larger, roughly the size of a gravestone. It sits on the floor as you come in, barring the way to the prettiness beyond, a slab of concrete with a snake in the middle. The snake is something big, a python or an anaconda, one of those deadly stranglers that squeeze the life out of you, except in this case he’s the one who is trapped.
The display ahead makes recurrent use of this same conceptual strategy. A curled-up yellow snake is trapped in ugly polystyrene packing. A spotty brown snake has been twisted into a question mark. A slither of multicoloured snake is briefly visible in a cracked block of yellow sandstone, like one of those gorgeous expanses of amethyst you find inside a lumpy geode.
So the snakes are imprisoned inside unpleasant expanses of packing material — polystyrene infill, concrete castings — but this heavy boxing can’t contain them; they keep bulging out and struggling. In her writings for the show, Morgan describes her artistic ambition as an effort to “whack-a-mole”; a hopeless attempt to contain something that keeps popping out. The snaky twists and knots are insistently intestinal. The sculptures may not look like us, but the relationship they record between squelchy insides and shiny outsides is our preferred relationship as well.
Also in the show is a set of creepy photo-works in which a female hand can be seen peeling the skin off a dead snake to reveal the gory flesh below. The peeling hand sports brightly painted fake nails of the kind you get expensively done on the high street. The Beyoncé nails turn the hands into talons. They’re entirely inappropriate for the job, but it’s very us to get them done that way.
The same message, then, on repeat: outsides say one thing, insides say another. Morgan points a finger at the Instagram age, at the urge to manipulate appearances and to hide the truth behind manufactured veneers. The truth won’t behave, is her point. The snakes won’t stop wriggling.
All this feels strikingly independent. The art reminds you of no one else. Hirst was macho, Morgan isn’t. The masculine territory of taxidermy has been commandeered by feminine intricacies and complex moods. Emotionally, in the atmospheres she creates, she’s nimble and light to the touch. Her art may consist largely of dead animals, but there’s no sense of death about it. Snakes have had a bad press ever since Genesis, but here they are presented as something elusive, beautiful, magical. As are the bits of hedgehog that make a couple of brief appearances and add textural variety to these slinky proceedings.
In the end, her art says something genuinely insightful about the modern world. She turns snakes into mirrors and holds them up to us. To do this with taxidermy is brave and special.
At the Royal Academy, the annual Summer Exhibition has finally arrived, rebranded as a Winter Exhibition. Having had to battle my way through this ghastly event on so many occasions, it gives me genuine pleasure to be able to report that this year’s effort is perhaps the best I’ve seen.
The problems are the usual ones — too much stuff, with too little focus, trying to survive in a stylistic mess — but for once the selected art seems mostly to have originated on the same planet as contemporary aesthetics. This is particularly true of the opening stretch, selected by Isaac Julien and devoted exclusively to black art.
This show within a show has some real high spots. The compelling Njideka Akunyili Crosby, in front of whose work I will always stop, has an extra-large figure piece in which a black woman cradles the head of a white man. Sonia Boyce, who is going to represent Britain at the next Venice Biennale, plucks catchy patterns out of the ether and combines them with haunting African faces. The exciting Zanele Muholi displays one of those towering self-portraits in which the masculine blurs seamlessly with the feminine.
All that is good. What isn’t good is the pricing of some of the art. Frankly, it’s obscene. Frank Bowling’s scrubby abstracted Watermelon Bight is on sale for £756,000! At the other end of the show, Ron Arad’s Oh Lord, Won’t You Buy Me? is yours for £324,000! The only people who can afford those prices are Russian oligarchs and Florida hedge-funders. What is the point of making art for them?
Polly Morgan: How to Behave at Home, the Bomb Factory, London N19, until Nov 2; Winter Exhibition, Royal Academy, London W1, until Jan 3

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.title: Move to Stroud, Gloucestershire
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.subtitle: House prices, schools and best streets to buy if you’re looking for a part-time commute — in the birthplace of Extinction Rebellion
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.text:
Flight from the city isn’t just about the wide-eyed pursuit of birdsong and breathable air. The urban escapees setting their sights on Stroud are every bit as focused on the traditional fundamentals of good schools and transport links as they are on its unrivalled sense of community and the lush Cotswold countryside all around.
There are certainly plenty of them. Gemma Goulding, manager of the local branch of Hamptons International estate agency, saw an 80 per cent increase in would-be buyers over the summer compared with last year. Although more than half are from London, plenty are coming from Bristol too. “So many people just don’t seem to want to live in a city any more,” she says.
Not that they’ll be cutting themselves off. London is 90 minutes away by train and Bristol a 45-minute drive. The schools are excellent — Stroud High and Marling are rated outstanding by Ofsted — and, Goulding says, there’s a wide choice of family houses in the £600,000 to £800,000 bracket that are right in the sweet spot for the stamp duty holiday.
Yet Stroud is about so much more than cold-eyed calculation.
If you’ve visited, you won’t be surprised to learn that Stroud was the birthplace of Extinction Rebellion. One glance at the Fortune Faeries shop — “dedicated to the preservation and protection of all Elemental Beings” — will tell you that this is one of those places where alternative ideas are allowed to flourish.
The farmers’ market (more on that later) is probably the country’s best, and the town centre is packed with arty, crafty independent shops, zero-waste stores and wholefood cafés, as well as highly visible community groups. The big event of the year is the Stroud Wassail, when morris dancers and mummers gather to see in the new year in semi-pagan style. Even the local football team, Forest Green Rovers, are vegan, with no animal products of any description for sale in the club, and a wooden stadium in the pipeline.
From certain angles Stroud could be a southern cousin of Hebden Bridge — all steep valleys, old mills and hippy trousers. There’s even a canal. Yet you don’t have to step far beyond the engagingly unpolished town centre to find yourself in the lush, posh heart of the Cotswolds. Like the jam in a tasty green doughnut, Stroud is surrounded by areas of outstanding natural beauty. It’s out in the sticks, close to the National Trust-owned playgrounds of Minchinhampton and Rodborough Commons, that you’ll find most of the famous names who have made their home around here: among them Zara Phillips and Mike Tindall, the comedy hellraiser Keith Allen and the actors Rafe Spall and Jamie Dornan.
Houses out here attract the highest prices — expect to pay from £650,000 to £1.5 million and beyond for a big family house. Convenience-seeking commuters are beginning to push up prices in the town. Here, family homes go for £400,000 or more, while two-bedroom flats — perhaps in a converted woollen mill — fetch about £200,000.
What brings town and country together is a love of good food and drink, from the delicious sourdough at Salt Bakehouse (about to launch an electric-bike delivery scheme) to the KFP burger (the P stands for pheasant) at the brilliant Jolly Nice Farmshop, in a converted garage on the A419. The star of the show, though, is the fantastic farmers’ market in Stroud. It’s still thriving, and displaying expert social distancing on an expanded site thanks to some judicious road closures. It’s one of the biggest in the country, with 50 stalls selling everything from cheese, bread and mushrooms to woodcarvings and weaving. It was the success of the market that inspired its founder, Jasper Conran, to describe Stroud as “the Covent Garden of the Cotswolds”. This oft-repeated quote seems entirely unfair to bohemian Stroud, which has a warmth and a spirit lacking in London’s corporate tourist shopping magnet.
Train Direct trains to London Paddington take 90 minutes, with a season ticket costing £290 a week or £10,600 a year. Cheltenham and Swindon are 30 minutes away by rail.
CarIt’s a half-hour drive north to Cheltenham or Gloucester, 45 minutes south to Bristol and 15 minutes west to the M5.
CyclingA new covered cycle store with room for 40 bikes opened last month, though cyclists be warned, Stroud is a hilly place.
BroadbandStroud is a little bit below average for superfast broadband coverage, and worse for ultrafast, according to thinkbroadband.com. Thanks to coverage in a number of villages from Gigaclear — a rural broadband provider — better speeds are available outside the town.
Air qualityNo problems.
SchoolingFor information on schooling, check our Parent Power guide
Cheltenham Road, £960,000Dating from the 17th century, this five-bedroom mill was built by a wealthy wool merchant. It oozes period charm, and has an attractive garden and a large outbuilding that makes it ideal for 21st-century working from home.01453 764912; hunters.com
Minchinhampton, £400,000This atmospheric three-bedroom, three-storey cottage is handily placed on the high street in Minchinhampton, one of Stroud’s smartest satellite villages. It has a courtyard garden with a useful utility room and cellar.01453 279 176; hamptons.co.uk
